scenarios.title: Why does the battery care about 0-100 km/h?
scenarios.blurb: Trace one driving expectation from a customer wish down to the two subsystems that deliver it, and the test that proves it.

steps.caption: A customer says: "I want brisk acceleration, 0 to 100 km/h." That's stakeholder requirement STK-003, Responsive Acceleration.
Engineering turns that wish into a system-level requirement: SYS-002, Propulsion Delivery. The whole drivetrain has to deliver that response.
Propulsion Delivery breaks into measurable requirements the powertrain must hit, including PERF-001, Tractive Force.
PERF-001 and its sibling PERF-002 (Electrical Traction Power) are both satisfied by the powertrain: the motor and gearbox that push the car forward.
Electrical Traction Power also derives a battery requirement: BAT-004, Traction Power Capability. The battery has to deliver that power on demand.
That's why 0-100 km/h is a battery concern, not just a motor one: the energy block satisfies BAT-004 right alongside the powertrain's requirements.
One test proves the whole chain: TC_ACCEL, Acceleration / Force / Power Verification, verifies the stakeholder wish and every requirement beneath it.

scenarios.title: What happens when you press the brake pedal?
scenarios.blurb: Follow one driver action from the pedal to the wheels, and to the battery that quietly recovers energy along the way.

steps.caption: You press the brake pedal. Physically, that command starts in the driver interface: the HMI block.
The pedal signal has to reach the right places correctly: IF-004, Brake Command Interface, is met jointly by the vehicle controller and the brakes.
That's part of a bigger promise: SYS-004, Controlled Braking, derived from the stakeholder need for safe, controlled transportation.
Controlled Braking is satisfied directly by the brakes, and also depends on the vehicle controller, powertrain, and battery working together.
Some of that braking is "blended": PERF-004, Regenerative Braking, is satisfied by the powertrain and the battery pack recovering energy instead of wasting it as heat.
BRK-002, Blended Braking, is the brake system's job: mix friction braking and regeneration so the pedal still feels smooth and predictable.
Two tests confirm it works: TC_BRAKE proves the friction brakes, TC_REGEN proves the energy recovery. One press, two systems, one confident stop.

scenarios.title: How do we know it is safe to charge?
scenarios.blurb: One customer wish, convenient charging, turns out to depend on three separate subsystems working together.

steps.caption: Customers want charging to be quick and hassle-free: STK-004, Convenient Charging.
That becomes SYS-008, Charge Management, owned by the charging port hardware itself.
Here's the charging port: the physical connection between the car and the wall.
But safety during charging isn't just the plug. The Battery Management System has to guard the cells: BAT-003, Battery Protection.
And the cooling system has to keep the battery at a safe temperature while it charges: THM-001, Battery Temperature Control.
TC_CHARGE proves charging itself performs as promised: speed, connection, everything the driver experiences.
TC_SAFETY proves the whole system is safe end to end, plug to pack. Three parts, one confident "safe to charge."

scenarios.title: One customer wish, many parts
scenarios.blurb: A single stakeholder requirement, safe controlled transportation, fans out across four different subsystems.

steps.caption: One simple customer wish: STK-001, Safe Controlled Transportation. Let's see how many parts of the car that actually touches.
It means the brakes must work reliably: SYS-004, Controlled Braking, satisfied by the brake block.
It also means the battery must never overheat: SYS-005, Thermal Control, satisfied by the cooling system.
It means high-voltage electricity must stay safely isolated: SYS-010, High-Voltage Isolation, satisfied by the energy storage block.
And if anything goes wrong, the vehicle controller must catch it: SYS-011, Fault Management.
Zoom out: one stakeholder wish became four system requirements, satisfied by four different subsystems: brakes, thermal, energy, and vehicle control.
Every one of those requirements still traces straight back to this same starting wish. Nothing is disconnected, that's the trace ladder in action.

scenarios.title: Nothing is forgotten
scenarios.blurb: Pick any part of the car at random: every one of them has requirements to meet and tests that prove it.

steps.caption: Start with the whole vehicle: 168 modeled elements and 13 physical parts, all traced from customer wishes to verification tests.
Take the diagnostics port, easy to overlook. It still owns 4 requirements, including SRV-001, Service Data Access, and 1 verification test, TC_DIAG.
The sensor suite: 4 requirements, SNS-001, SNS-002, IF-003, and SYS-006, verified by 2 tests, TC_INTERFACE and TC_STATE.
The charging port again: 4 requirements, 1 test, TC_CHARGE. Same pattern, every time, on every part.
Every part has an owner. Every requirement has a test.
